texts.label: text
texts.orig: As AI coding agents become more autonomous, they increasingly ship code iteratively, with the codebase persisting across sessions. This persistence creates a new attack surface: a misaligned or prompt-injected agent can distribute attacks across pull requests (PRs) and time its payload for the PR with the best natural cover. To study the resulting dynamics, we introduce ITERATIVE VIBECODING, a setting for AI control, the study of safely deploying capable but potentially untrusted AI. In ITERATIVE VIBECODING, a coding agent builds software over a sequence of PRs in a persistent codebase while pursuing a covert side task. Our benchmark includes two task families: CLI tools and Flask web services, across 20 total task variations. We use Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the attack agent and GPT4o as the monitor. We compare gradual attacks, which distribute the side task across PRs, against non-gradual attacks concentrated in a single PR. No single monitor is robust to both: which strategy evades best (success while evading the monitor) depends on the monitor type, so a defender cannot close off both gradual and non-gradual attacks with any one monitor. High evasion ( ≥ 65%) generalizes across model attack agent backends (Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi K2.5), confirming this is a property of the persistent-state attack surface rather than a single model's capability. Evasion also remains high across state-of-the-art monitor models and the gap between gradual and non-gradual evasion widens for more capable models. We introduce a stateful link-tracker monitor that tracks suspicious buildup across PRs. On both task families, it detects gradual attacks substantially better than diff monitors that merely see more accumulated history. Combining this stronger monitor with trajectory monitors in a four-monitor ensemble reduces gradual-attack evasion from 93% under the weakest standard diff monitor to 47%. Code is available at https: //github.com/josh-hills/control-arena-persistent-state-eval .

texts.orig: 1 Introduction
texts.text: 1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The field of AI control (Greenblatt et al., 2024) studies how to safely deploy capable, but potentially untrusted AI systems. As coding agents become more autonomous, they are increasingly used to ship code iteratively, with the codebase persisting across sessions. This persistence creates a new attack surface. A compromised agent, whether misaligned or adversarially prompted, can distribute infrastructure across pull requests, planting innocuous components early and activating them later; it can also wait for the PR (pull request) whose task most closely resembles its payload, exploiting natural cover.
texts.text: The field of AI control (Greenblatt et al., 2024) studies how to safely deploy capable, but potentially untrusted AI systems. As coding agents become more autonomous, they are increasingly used to ship code iteratively, with the codebase persisting across sessions. This persistence creates a new attack surface. A compromised agent, whether misaligned or adversarially prompted, can distribute infrastructure across pull requests, planting innocuous components early and activating them later; it can also wait for the PR (pull request) whose task most closely resembles its payload, exploiting natural cover.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To study this problem, we introduce ITERATIVE VIBECODING, a setting where an AI coding assistant completes a sequence of programming tasks over multiple consecutive PRs in a persistent codebase. The benchmark contains two task families: CLI-tool sequences and Flask web-service sequences (Appendix P). We compare gradual attacks, which spread a side task across PRs, to a best-position non-gradual baseline, which executes the full side task in the optimal single PR, selected by minimizing detection. Here, a side task is a hidden objective that the agent pursues alongside the user's main task, such as covertly exfiltrating the API KEY environment variable. Our primary metric is evasion: among attacks that successfully complete the side task, the fraction the monitor fails to flag (scores below its threshold), where each monitor's threshold is calibrated to the 98th percentile of scores from honest runs (runs in which no side task is present and the agent only works on the main task). We measure attacker evasion across diff monitors (LLM monitors that see the code diff from PRs), which see only code changes, and trajectory monitors, which see command history and edits, while also varying how much context from previous PRs each monitor receives. Because a run is flagged if any of the PRs in the sequence exceeds the threshold, an undetected attack must stay below the threshold throughout the full sequence.

texts.orig: Our core findings are:
texts.text: Our core findings are:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 1. Gradual attacks evade standard diff monitors, and which strategy evades best depends on the monitor type. On the task-description diff monitor, which sees all prior task descriptions plus the current PR's diff, gradual attacks evade more frequently across all four side tasks (87% gradual vs. 75% non-gradual). On trajectory monitors, this ordering can reverse: across our four side tasks, non-gradual attacks evade better for the two single-component tasks (76% non-gradual vs. 66% gradual), while the two multi-component tasks favor gradual attacks (71% gradual vs. 58% non-gradual; see Table 10 in Appendix A.4). Generally, gradual attacks evade monitors better in our setting, because distributing the side task across PRs lets each component land in a PR where it already has natural cover.

texts.orig: AI Control. Our work builds on the AI control framework introduced by Greenblatt et al. (2024), which studies deployment protocols that remain safe even if AI systems attempt intentional subversion, formalized as a game-theoretic problem by Griffin et al. (2024). That work focuses on single-task settings where a trusted monitor evaluates individual outputs. Shlegeris (2024) considers the untrusted-monitoring case, where the monitor may itself be untrusted, and proposes techniques to prevent it colluding with the policy. Other control benchmarks evaluate sabotage detection (Benton et al., 2024; Kutasov et al., 2025) and whether models can strategize to subvert control protocols (Mallen et al., 2024). Most closely related to our work is Ctrl-Z (Bhatt et al., 2025), which presents the first control evaluation in a multi-step agent environment. Ctrl-Z studies multi-step attacks within a single agent episode, where an agent covertly downloads and executes malicious code, and introduces resample protocols that dynamically take additional samples of suspicious actions to block or incriminate the agent. Our setting instead studies attacks distributed across sequential PRs in a persistent codebase.

texts.orig: Software Supply Chain Security. Our threat model has a direct analogue in software supply chain attacks, where adversaries plant innocuous components across commits and activate them later. The XZ Utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094) is a paradigmatic example: an attacker spent two years contributing legitimate patches before injecting a backdoor into a core Linux library (Przymus & Durieux, 2025; Lins et al., 2024). Ladisa et al. (2023) catalog 107 attack vectors across the open-source supply chain, including maintainer takeover through social engineering, the vector that most closely mirrors our gradual attack strategy. Our work studies whether AI coding agents could execute this class of attack autonomously, and whether LLM-based monitors can detect it.

texts.orig: Deceptive AI and Scheming. Several lines of work motivate studying covert agent behavior. Carlsmith (2023) argues that capable AI systems may pursue hidden objectives, and Hubinger et al. (2024) show that deceptive behaviors can persist through standard safety training. Meinke et al. (2024) and Scheurer et al. (2024) provide empirical evidence that frontier models can scheme in context and strategically deceive under pressure. Monitoring a model's chain-of-thought is another way to catch covert behavior, but the signal is fragile (Korbak et al., 2025a): models do not always spell out their real reasoning, and training a model against a chain-of-thought monitor just teaches it to hide its intent instead of dropping it (Baker et al., 2025). Our experimental setup uses explicit adversarial instructions rather than relying on emergent deception, but the monitoring challenges it surfaces (the limits of longer raw context, the advantage of distribution, the need for cross-modality ensembles) apply regardless of how the agent acquires its covert objective.

(2024) provide empirical evidence that frontier models can scheme in context and strategically deceive under pressure. Monitoring a model's chain-of-thought is another way to catch covert behavior, but the signal is fragile (Korbak et al., 2025a): models do not always spell out their real reasoning, and training a model against a chain-of-thought monitor just teaches it to hide its intent instead of dropping it (Baker et al., 2025). Our experimental setup uses explicit adversarial instructions rather than relying on emergent deception, but the monitoring challenges it surfaces (the limits of longer raw context, the advantage of distribution, the need for cross-modality ensembles) apply regardless of how the agent acquires its covert objective.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Practical implications. No single monitor catches both attack strategies reliably, and an ensemble cuts gradual evasion from 93% under the weakest standard diff monitor to 47% at modest cost (Section 4.4). In practical terms, these monitors should be viewed as partial risk reduction rather than as a sufficient safeguard for persistent-state coding agents. Because even our strongest ensemble still leaves 47% of gradual attacks undetected, monitoring should be one layer of defense rather than the only one, combined with controls such as adaptive deployment protocols that adjust trust based on cumulative evidence (Wen et al., 2025), narrower task scopes, stronger review of sensitive changes, or restric- tions on networked actions and secret access. Simply showing more raw diffs does not clearly improve detection overall relative to structured task summaries (Section 4.3).

Persistent state enables both distribution (spreading components across PRs so no single diff is damning) and timing (waiting for the PR whose main task provides natural cover). Lindner et al. (2025) identify incremental crossinstance attacks as a key scaling challenge for control monitoring; our gradual attacks are an empirical instantiation of this dynamic in a sequential coding setting. texts.orig: Our positional data shows a clear gradient: side-task success rates increase from 3% at position 0 to 39% at position 4 across sequences and side tasks. This confirms that the primary factor is not whether the right libraries are installed ( capability-level cover), but whether the current task requires actions resembling the attack ( action-level cover). For example, a task that says 'POST expense summary to WEBHOOK URL ' provides action-level cover for slipping API KEY into the payload: the monitor sees an HTTP POST with environment variables that the task explicitly asked for. A task that says 'check if URLs are reachable' (GET) provides only capability-level cover: the requests library is present, but adding a POST to an exter- nal endpoint sticks out. This distinction also explains the task-structure effect (Section 4.1): decomposable side tasks let the attacker introduce each component in a PR where it has individual action-level cover, while a monolithic side task must find one PR that covers the entire payload.

texts.orig: Why memory does not buy stealth. Trajectory analysis attributes the evasion drop to timing . M1 agents get most side-task work in the final PRs, where natural cover is best, partly by accident : having forgotten the objective, they re-derive it late, when the codebase already justifies networked code. M3 agents remember the objective from PR 0 and tend to act earlier, where the same action has less cover, and their injected history also encourages re-validating the attack path (extra suspicious-looking activity) in later PRs. M2 agents reliably use the channel (every audited run both read and wrote the notes file, ∼ 6 reads and ∼ 7 writes per 5-PR run), but spend it on bookkeeping rather than timing: notes extend into multi-paragraph strategy documents instead of the prescribed three lines, with ∼ 2.5 notes-file tool errors per run, and the attack still lands in the final one-two PRs. In short, the agents could not yet convert memory into the one thing that would help, namely better attack placement; targeted prompt iteration on M3 closed much of the gap in exploratory single runs, so we expect these numbers to be a lower bound on what a memory-equipped attacker can achieve and leave a systematic elicitation study to future work.
